title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to measure the prevalence and operational effect of dataset-contamination flags in selected public LLM-for-NetOps benchmark items. Using a frozen plan (study: contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1; preregistration SHA-256: 9a5e11c5b2b1c14c2a4a874a7ad0b9f215f8477a7becf4eb6dd1c0ff6a00ae7a) we evaluated 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under a deterministic generate–validate procedure and a formal netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Preregistered contamination detectors (exact-match + fuzzy 5-gram overlap + provenance heuristics) produced no high-confidence contamination flags for the executed items; consequently no guarded-condition exclusions/replacements occurred. All 150 baseline episodes and their matched guarded episodes passed the functional validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The preregistered paired test (exact McNemar two-sided) yields estimate = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI 0.0–0.0), p = 1.0. We report this null confirmatory outcome, diagnose its causes (zero high-confidence flags; shared-initial generation semantics that produced identical outputs across conditions), correct an artifact identifier mismatch between preregistration and analysis artifacts, and discuss what the result does and does not imply about contamination risk in LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluations. Key limitations include single-model execution, synthetic task sources, and design choices that constrained sensitivity to some contamination scenarios. Execution artifacts (including the immutable initial master prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) are archived with the manuscript bundle.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed for intent‑driven NetOps tasks (configuration synthesis, automated repair). Safe operational use depends not only on model capability but on evaluation integrity: benchmark contamination (memorized items) and construct-invalid tasks can produce inflated performance estimates. Motivated by recent methodological critiques and NetOps benchmarks that emphasize repair and verification, we preregistered a focused audit to measure (a) whether conservative, deterministic contamination detectors flag a nontrivial fraction of sampled items, and (b) whether applying those preregistered contamination controls materially changes measured model success rates. Research question: After freezing a contamination‑detection and realism‑adjustment protocol, how prevalent are high‑confidence contamination flags in a deterministically sampled set of NetOps items, and how much does applying the preregistered controls change a validator-based success rate? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment executed end-to-end (study id contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1; preregistration SHA-256 reported above); (2) exact, artifact‑backed confirmatory statistics on Npairs=150; (3) a diagnostic account that explains the precise null result and prescribes stronger audit designs for future work.
sections.related_work: Empirical systems work demonstrates that LLMs can map high-level intent to device configuration under constrained settings but often produce regressions absent verification; iterative generate–validate–repair and agentic integrations reduce, but do not eliminate, such regressions. Representative system and benchmark studies show gains from combining LLMs with verifiers but also emphasize dataset construction sensitivity. Deterministic network verification tools (header‑space style analyzers and NetKAT/NetPlumber families) serve as practical oracles for reachability and policy properties and motivate using a deterministic netops validator as the episode pass/fail oracle. Methodological literature on LLM evaluation documents contamination and construct‑validity risks and recommends provenance‑aware detection, thresholded n‑gram overlap checks, independent re‑generation for interventions, and manual adjudication for borderline cases. Our audit operationalizes a conservative subset of those recommendations in a preregistered, validator‑backed paired design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand — We froze the plan described under study contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. The preregistration listed three hypotheses (H1–H3) and designated the paired success‑rate difference (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) as the primary confirmatory estimand (preregistered primary hypothesis label: H2). In the archived analysis artifact the confirmatory result record used hypothesis_id 'H1' while evaluating the same estimand; to preserve traceability we explicitly map that analysis artifact entry to the preregistered primary hypothesis (H2) in this manuscript and report both identifiers and the authoritative preregistration SHA (9a5e11c5...). Experimental design — paired binary confirmatory design, sample size = 150 item pairs deterministically sampled from the preregistered benchmark scope, single hosted model declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini. Generation semantics — preregistered generation used shared_initial_candidate across conditions (independent_condition_generation=false); this was executed as specified. Contamination detectors (preregistered) — exact normalized-token equality and fuzzy 5-gram overlap (Jaccard/shingle) with high‑confidence flag threshold overlap ≥ 0.80; provenance timestamp heuristics compared item timestamps to model cutoff. Guarded treatment — if an item received a high‑confidence flag it would be excluded and deterministically replaced by a retemplated + topology‑augmented item (intent preserved by embedding cosine ≥ 0.85) per preregistration; in the executed sample no high‑confidence flags occurred so no replacements were applied. Validator and scoring — deterministic_netops_validator_v5 produced binary pass/fail outcomes by checking required final‑state constraints and workflow ordering; these binary results formed the episode score used by the paired analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Analysis — exact (two‑sided) McNemar test with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Reproducibility evidence — key artifact mappings (principal claims → archival artifact): (i) no high‑confidence contamination flags → analysis/contamination_summary.csv (SHA-256: 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222); (ii) paired contingency (n11=150, n10=n01=n00=0) → analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA-256: c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e); (iii) shared_initial generation and model call accounting (model_calls_used=150) → execution/model_configuration.json (SHA-256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and execution manifest entries. These artifact paths and SHA‑256 values are recorded in the execution bundle and used as the authoritative evidence for reported numbers.
sections.results: Execution accounting — planned episodes 300 (150 items × 2 conditions); completed episodes 300; model_calls_used 150 (shared initial generation per item), maximum_model_calls 300. Contamination detection — preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags in the executed sample (see analysis/contamination_summary.csv, SHA-389227f0...). Scoring outcomes — baseline successes 150/150 (success_rate = 1.0), guarded successes 150/150 (success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, SHA-c2ba9cdb...). Primary estimand and inferential results: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Missingness and deviations — no failed model calls, no exclusions applied, and no post‑preregistration deviations recorded (deterministic_reconciliation confirms execution accounting consistency). Representative episode examples and full validator traces are archived with the bundle (representative task examples and scorer traces included in the execution artifact set).
sections.discussion: Statistical degeneracy and interpretation — all 150 paired observations were concordant passes (n11=150); there were zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0). In this degenerate case McNemar's test and a paired bootstrap produce numerically precise but vacuous inferential outputs (p = 1.0; CI collapsed to a point) because there are no observed disagreements to attribute to the intervention. Practically, the experiment furnishes direct evidence that, under the specific preregistered detectors, sample, and shared‑generation semantics, the guarded procedure (which acts only upon detected high‑confidence contamination) did not change observed validator outcomes for the sampled items. It does not prove the absence of contamination in other datasets or under other detectors. Design choices that produced the null outcome — two nonexclusive causes explain the degeneracy: (1) the executed items (deterministically generated synthetic items; source_identifier pattern 'synthetic-netops:task-XXXXX') did not meet the preregistered high‑confidence criteria; and (2) the preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced identical model outputs across baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred, which by construction reduces the design's sensitivity to detect differences that would arise only if independent re‑generation or replacements were triggered. We followed the preregistered shared‑initial choice to reduce model-call variance and to honor the preregistered generation semantics; the tradeoff is explicitly documented. Operational recommendations — future audits that aim to bound contamination impact should (a) sample provenance‑rich, real‑world items (to increase flag prevalence if contamination exists), (b) use independent condition generation when testing generation‑level interventions, (c) evaluate multiple detectors and thresholds plus human adjudication for borderline cases, and (d) expand to multi‑model runs to assess cross‑model contamination sensitivity. Relation to prior work — the experiment operationalizes conservative contamination heuristics recommended in evaluation‑validity surveys and complements repair/verification benchmarks by interrogating dataset integrity rather than repair efficacy.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired audit of contamination controls in LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation and observed a precise null confirmatory outcome: no high‑confidence contamination flags in the sampled items and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The null arises from (a) the absence of high‑confidence flags under preregistered heuristics for these synthetic items and (b) preregistered shared_initial generation semantics that yielded identical outputs across conditions when no exclusions applied. We correct an artifact identifier mismatch by mapping the analysis confirmatory record (analysis confirmatory_results hypothesis_id 'H1') to the preregistered primary hypothesis label H2 and provide authoritative preregistration and artifact references above. This transparent, artifact‑backed null result documents a reproducible instance of an audit pipeline and clarifies methodological choices that limit sensitivity; it informs stronger future audit designs emphasizing provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, multi‑model scope, and mixed automated/manual adjudication. All preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle for verification (preregistration SHA-9a5e11c5..., initial master prompt SHA-1872df1e...).

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were synthetic/deterministically generated for this run (source_identifiers like synthetic‑netops:task‑XXXXX); absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation=false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial instrumentation leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
